main_contribution: Provides a process model for problem identification, artifact design, demonstration, evaluation, and communication.
main_limitation_or_critique: Methodology source, not dashboard evaluation evidence by itself.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Structure artifact chapter.
supports_claim: The dashboard should be presented as a designed and demonstrated artifact, not decoration.

authors: Chen, Hsinchun and Chiang, Roger H. L. and Storey, Veda C.
title: Business Intelligence and Analytics: From Big Data to Big Impact
bucket: Design science, dashboard, and decision-support artifact framing
main_contribution: Frames analytics as a business-impact and decision-support discipline.
main_limitation_or_critique: Broad analytics source, not a distress model paper.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Positions thesis under business analytics/big data.
supports_claim: The project belongs to business analytics because it translates data/model outputs into decision support.

authors: Shneiderman, Ben
title: The Eyes Have It: A Task by Data Type Taxonomy for Information Visualizations
publication: Proceedings of the IEEE Symposium on Visual Languages
bucket: Design science, dashboard, and decision-support artifact framing
main_contribution: Supports overview, zoom/filter, and details-on-demand logic.
main_limitation_or_critique: Visualization principle, not financial content.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Justifies dashboard layout and filters.
supports_claim: Interactive filtering and drill-down are not cosmetic; they support analytical workflow.

authors: Arnott, David and Pervan, Graham
title: A Critical Analysis of Decision Support Systems Research Revisited: The Rise of Design Science
bucket: Design science, dashboard, and decision-support artifact framing
main_contribution: Links decision support systems research with design science approaches.
main_limitation_or_critique: Methodological source, not empirical distress evidence.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports dashboard as a decision-support system.
supports_claim: The artifact should be evaluated by usefulness and transparency, not only model metrics.

authors: Barney, Jay
title: Firm Resources and Sustained Competitive Advantage
bucket: Strategic management and resilience framing
main_contribution: Frames persistent firm differences and resource advantages.
main_limitation_or_critique: Does not directly measure SEC ratios or failure targets.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: High-level success/resilience framing only.
supports_claim: Firm-level heterogeneity matters for success and resilience.

authors: Teece, David J. and Pisano, Gary and Shuen, Amy
title: Dynamic Capabilities and Strategic Management
bucket: Strategic management and resilience framing
main_contribution: Explains adaptation and capability renewal under changing environments.
main_limitation_or_critique: The thesis measures financial signals, not capabilities directly.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Frames market shifts and adaptation without overclaiming unobserved capabilities.
supports_claim: Adaptation is relevant to the title, but empirical measurement is through observable financial resilience.

authors: Hannan, Michael T. and Freeman, John
title: Structural Inertia and Organizational Change
bucket: Strategic management and resilience framing
main_contribution: Explains why organizations may have difficulty adapting under environmental shifts.
main_limitation_or_critique: Sociological theory, not financial ratio modeling.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Frames failure under market shifts conceptually.
supports_claim: Failure and survival are linked to adaptation constraints, but the thesis measures only financial outcomes.

authors: Duchek, Stephanie
title: Organizational Resilience: A Capability-Based Conceptualization
bucket: Strategic management and resilience framing
main_contribution: Conceptualizes resilience as capabilities for anticipation, coping, and adaptation.
main_limitation_or_critique: Does not provide financial-target definitions for public firms.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports naming the success target as resilience with caveats.
supports_claim: Resilience is conceptually broader than profitability, so the thesis must define a measurable financial proxy.

authors: Hepfer, Martin and Lawrence, Thomas B.
title: The Heterogeneity of Organizational Resilience: Exploring Functional, Operational and Strategic Resilience
bucket: Strategic management and resilience framing
main_contribution: Differentiates forms of resilience rather than treating resilience as one simple outcome.
main_limitation_or_critique: Not a financial prediction model.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports careful wording around success/resilience target.
supports_claim: The thesis uses financial resilience as a proxy, not a complete measure of organizational resilience.

authors: Linnenluecke, Martina K.
title: Resilience in Business and Management Research: A Review of Influential Publications and a Research Agenda
bucket: Strategic management and resilience framing
main_contribution: Reviews resilience concepts in business and management literature.
main_limitation_or_critique: Broad review; not a direct measurement recipe for SEC data.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Literature anchor for resilience framing.
supports_claim: Resilience is a recognized management construct, but operationalization must be explicit.

authors: Charalambakis, Evangelos and Garrett, Ian
title: On the Prediction of Financial Distress in Developed and Emerging Markets: Does the Choice of Accounting and Market Information Matter? A Comparison of UK and Indian Firms
publication: Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting
bucket: Emerging-market and Russia-specific distress prediction context
main_method_or_theory: hazard model; accounting and market predictor comparison
data_scope: UK and Indian firms; developed versus emerging market comparison
main_contribution: Shows that the predictive value of accounting and market variables can differ across institutional settings: market variables help in the UK case, while accounting ratios dominate in India.
main_limitation_or_critique: Compares the UK and India, not Russia or the implemented U.S. SEC/FRED panel; it uses a different model family and does not build a dashboard or target hierarchy.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports the literature-review claim that distress predictors are not perfectly portable across institutional settings and that market-context variables need careful empirical validation.
supports_claim: Institutional context can change the usefulness of accounting versus market information in distress prediction.

authors: Hunter, John and Isachenkova, Natalia
title: Failure Risk: A Comparative Study of UK and Russian Firms
bucket: Emerging-market and Russia-specific distress prediction context
main_method_or_theory: logit failure-risk model; bootstrap validation; UK-Russia comparison
data_scope: Russian industrial firms from the transition period and a comparable UK recession-period sample
main_contribution: Provides direct Russia-specific comparative evidence that failure predictors differ between Russian and UK firms, with profitability more dominant in Russia while gearing and liquidity are more prominent in the UK context.
main_limitation_or_critique: Older transition-economy period, small Russian sample, narrow historical context, and different data environment from the current U.S. SEC/FRED panel.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports the contextual claim that Russian firm-failure prediction may require different predictor interpretation and should not simply import Western predictor assumptions.
supports_claim: Russian corporate failure predictors may differ from developed-market predictors; cross-country transferability is limited.

authors: Afanasev, Vladislav
title: Default Prediction Model for Emerging Capital Market Service Companies
bucket: Emerging-market and Russia-specific distress prediction context
main_method_or_theory: logistic regression, random forest, and k-nearest neighbors
data_scope: 404 Russian service firms and 304 developed European service-firm controls
main_contribution: Tests whether financial-data-only default prediction is less accurate for Russian service companies than for developed European controls, finding higher prediction error for Russian firms and suggesting financial ratios alone may be insufficient.
main_limitation_or_critique: Service-sector only; financial-ratio-only design; not a broad cross-industry macro-regime panel; not the same target hierarchy as this thesis.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports a Russia-specific literature paragraph explaining why contextual variables and careful scope limits matter in emerging capital-market settings.
supports_claim: Russian default prediction is feasible but may behave differently from developed-market prediction, especially if only financial ratios are used.

authors: Fedorova, Elena A.; Musienko, Svetlana O.; Fedorov, Fedor Yu.
title: Analysis of the External Factors Influence on the Forecasting of Bankruptcy of Russian Companies
publication: St Petersburg University Journal of Economic Studies
bucket: Emerging-market and Russia-specific distress prediction context
main_method_or_theory: binary-choice bankruptcy prediction models with internal and external factor blocks
data_scope: Russian construction, manufacturing, and trading companies; sector-specific bankruptcy samples
main_contribution: Shows that adding external macroeconomic factors such as GDP growth, key rate, exchange rates, CPI, MICEX growth, and unemployment can improve bankruptcy-prediction explanatory capacity for Russian companies relative to internal factors alone.
main_limitation_or_critique: Russian-language source; sector samples and modeling details differ from the current U.S. SEC/FRED design; supports external-factor relevance, not the exact market-health index.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports the market-shift/macro-context logic in a Russia-specific setting and helps justify future Russian macro-regime variables.
supports_claim: External macro factors can matter for Russian bankruptcy prediction and may improve models beyond internal company variables.

authors: Nevredinov, Aleksandr R.
title: The Instrumental Machine Learning Methods for Corporate Bankruptcy Prediction
bucket: Emerging-market and Russia-specific distress prediction context
main_method_or_theory: machine-learning method development and data-source review for bankruptcy prediction
main_contribution: Shows that Russian bankruptcy prediction has an active machine-learning methodological stream and discusses data sources, model potential, and input selection for company analysis.
main_limitation_or_critique: Less central than empirical cross-country/Russian sector papers; methodological/applied framing may be weaker for theory; peer-review status should be checked before heavy reliance.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Use as a secondary local-context source showing that ML-based bankruptcy prediction is recognized in Russian applied finance literature.
supports_claim: Russian bankruptcy-prediction research includes ML methods, so novelty should not be framed as simply using ML.

authors: Gornostaev, Dmitry; Ponomarenko, Alexey; Seleznev, Sergei; Sterkhova, Aleksandra
title: A Real-Time Historical Database of Macroeconomic Indicators for Russia
publication: Russian Journal of Money and Finance
bucket: Official data sources and empirical context
data_scope: Russian short-term macroeconomic indicators and data revisions
main_contribution: Documents a Russian macroeconomic vintage database and shows that revisions can be substantial, supporting the importance of using information available at the time rather than revised data.
main_limitation_or_critique: Macro-data infrastructure source, not a firm-level distress model; relevant mainly if a Russian macro panel or future extension is discussed.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Supports timing/revision logic for any future Russian macro-regime extension and reinforces the general thesis emphasis on prediction-date validity.
supports_claim: Real-time macro-data availability matters when building historically valid predictive models.

authors: Davydov, A. Yu.
title: US and Russian Financial Markets: Comparative Analysis
bucket: Macroeconomic conditions, credit cycles, and market-shift/default context
main_contribution: Provides background evidence that Russian and U.S. financial markets differ structurally, supporting caution when transferring market-shift assumptions across countries.
main_limitation_or_critique: Financial-market comparison, not firm-level distress prediction; should be background only.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Use as a secondary macro-financial context source if discussing why Russia and the U.S. should not be treated as interchangeable empirical environments.
supports_claim: Cross-country market structure differences can affect how market variables should be interpreted.

authors: Bank of Russia
title: Financial Stability
publication: Bank of Russia official financial stability portal
bucket: Official data sources and empirical context
main_method_or_theory: official financial-stability monitoring and macroprudential context
data_scope: Russian financial stability reviews, macroprudential policy, stress testing, analytics, and related materials
main_contribution: Defines and documents the Bank of Russia financial-stability monitoring context, including shocks, vulnerabilities, resilience, and macroprudential/stress-testing materials.
main_limitation_or_critique: Official context source, not peer-reviewed literature and not firm-level distress evidence.
how_this_thesis_uses_it: Use only if discussing a possible Russian macro-stability extension or official Russian macro-financial context.
supports_claim: Russian official sources exist for constructing macro-financial regime context in a future Russian extension.
